name: Victor Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, 43, and I lead home and business wiring jobs and the difficult repair calls. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest practical workers at the firm, though my pay is typical. My partner works at a laundry; we have children aged thirteen and sixteen, a mortgage and two months of expenses saved. There are some other electrical firms nearby, but the current rewiring contract ends in December and the next paid rota isn't confirmed; I've never used AI and prefer my test book and a method I can explain beside the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can get back to the job rather than another presentation. I've never used AI and I don't want a subscription attached to everything I do. Give me a clear drawing, a test book and somebody who answers the phone when the site changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be anxious about our paid days after December, when the firm's current rewiring contract ends. My wage is typical and our bills are covered now, with two months of expenses saved, but the next rota isn't confirmed. I can be very good at a repair and still not know which paid project follows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the wiring and repair work. This week I'd ask the owner which January days and rate were actually confirmed, rather than assume the next job had followed because the last one went well. Through the first year I'd bring lunch from home and deposit the 30 monthly saved after food costs only while actual wages covered essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the gap in the diary, with relief that the tools and work remain familiar. Two months saved lets me compare choices without a panic call tonight. It doesn't make an unconfirmed rota into income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you the person leading the jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm one of the strongest practical electricians here. I lead awkward home and business work and check the crew's final results. I'm happy to teach a method beside somebody, but I don't use AI to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares the household plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner works at a laundry, our children are thirteen and sixteen, and we have a mortgage. There are some other electrical firms nearby, but I don't have an offer from one in my pocket. We'd rather check actual wages and travel than tell each other my reputation is another savings account.

I'd keep **practical teaching** beside the work rather than use AI I have never tried.
think: Our **current wage** covers bills, but January paid days remain unconfirmed after the December contract ends.
Two months saved gives **comparison time**, while strong practical skill doesn't make the next project paid work yet.
do: Keep **leading repairs** and checking crew work through the first year.
Ask now about **confirmed January days** and rate, treating the rest as uncertain.
Save **30 monthly** from bringing lunch only after food costs and while actual wages cover essentials.
feel: **Anxious** about an unconfirmed paid rota, with a moderate cushion that prevents an immediate panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can try its systems, but it needs to show where the quoted time came from. I'd ask for the proposed jobs on paper and compare them with work we've finished. I don't want the apprentice blamed because a neat timetable couldn't get behind a real cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid planning time or job allowance could shrink even though the wiring still needs hands. That comes on top of the next contract not being confirmed, so it matters to our household. My partner's laundry work is physical too, but I won't use another wage as an excuse to ignore a cut in mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join two colleagues this month in a written request for consultation before paid-hour changes and for practical checking time to stay paid. I'd compare the office's printed plans with our actual completed-job times, without using the AI system myself. During the first year I'd keep paid repair work and save the lunch money only after food and essential bills were covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, and irritated if asking for a printed explanation is treated as being awkward. I can read a job and a wage offer without wanting to operate every new screen. I'd rather be slow to approve a number than quick to excuse a wrong one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the joint request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid hours and rate, the time needed for checks, and a discussion before either changed. We'd ask the owner to respond in writing. Signing together wouldn't mean the terms were already protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a printed plan that missed access work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show the actual time and the notes from the completed job, then ask for the allowance to be corrected before the next promise to a customer. I'd keep the safety checks instead of squeezing them to make the plan look right. A printed page isn't true just because I prefer paper.

I'd protect **apprentice checks** instead of blame a worker for impossible access or timing.
think: My **paid planning time** or job allowance could shrink while the physical wiring still needs doing.
That risk adds to **unconfirmed future work**, and my partner's physical job doesn't make a cut in my wage harmless.
do: Sign a **joint request** now for consultation before changes and paid time for practical checks.
Compare **printed plans** with completed-job times without operating the AI system.
Keep **paid repairs** during the first year and save 30 monthly only after food costs and essentials.
feel: **Anxious** about own earnings, with irritation at resistance being mistaken for inability to judge a job.

steps.text: Sign joint request for consultation on hours and paid practical checking time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031, so a person with tools isn't outside the picture. I'd tell the crew to check actual paid work, not rely on a title. I'd tell the children we're planning without making them choose an occupation to calm us down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the robots to remove a large share of the ordinary installation hours that support my wage. Difficult faults could still exist, but I don't expect enough paid calls for every displaced crew. Two months saved helps with a short gap, not a long fall in household income when my partner's laundry work is physical too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply now to posted crew-lead electrical roles while keeping the current wage. I'd leave only with signed written pay and guaranteed paid hours covering our bills after travel, with my partner agreeing changed care duties. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep whichever paid repair job I actually had, and ask the lender about eligibility and full costs if actual household income missed mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large later wage loss, even with a list of applications to make. I wake up thinking of the mortgage amount and the jobs I can't promise. I'd rather admit I need a real offer than say my licence makes the future owe me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an application lead you to check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual tasks, written wage, guaranteed paid hours and travel costs, then what shifts meant for the care we shared. I'd keep the existing wage until an affordable signed offer existed. A new company name isn't evidence that the work escapes robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would asking the lender mean changing the payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what options existed and what eligibility, fees and later costs applied. My partner and I would keep the existing payment in the budget unless we both agreed to actual written terms. I'd never treat a possible option as approved support.

Our **two-month reserve** covers a short gap, while my partner's physical work also faces the later endpoint.

Leave only with **written pay** and guaranteed hours covering bills after travel and my partner agreeing changed care duties.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and ask the lender about eligibility and full costs if actual income misses payments.
feel: **Alarmed** about an expected large later wage loss, with sleeplessness despite active applications and a usable buffer.
S2.quote: A new company name isn't evidence that the work escapes robots.
fieldNote: His **actual applications** use existing high skill and retain signed affordable pay, guaranteed hours, travel costs and partner-agreed care.
The **lender inquiry** preserves eligibility, full costs and both adults' agreement to written changes; no payment relief is assumed.

steps.text: Apply now for posted electrical crew-lead roles while retaining the current wage
Leave only with signed pay and guaranteed hours covering bills after travel, plus partner's care agreement
Keep actual paid repair work after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to ask for a more dependable agreement, not only a new qualification. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, then robots around 2034. I'd ask what paid hours the employer can actually promise while we use the skills we already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031, with children about eighteen and twenty-one, but I don't know what help they'd still need. The current gap after December would still be my starting problem today. More years gives me time to compare a contract without pretending the next mortgage payment has moved into the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign a staff request now for written minimum paid hours with the current weekly wage protected. If the employer refused, I'd apply to posted crew-lead roles, leaving only with signed pay and guaranteed hours covering bills after travel and my partner's care agreement. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep actual paid repairs and continue applications only if the paid hours still failed our household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money, with more room for a careful argument and a real search. I'm not against ordinary learning; I just don't want another course sold as the answer to an unconfirmed wage. I'd start with the paid work and terms I can understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would signing the request change your contract immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask for an employer answer in writing and use the actual present terms until something was agreed. If no better agreement came, I'd keep the existing wage while applying. A request doesn't put a minimum number of paid days into the diary by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume a stronger contract protected you forever?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd read what it actually said and keep checking the work. Capable robots around 2034 still reach physical tasks in your picture. I'd rather have clearer current terms than pretend a contract can predict every later market.

I'd ask about **actual promised hours** while continuing work that uses the skills we already have.

The **December contract ending** remains today's problem despite more time before thinking AI and robots.

His **resistant preference** favours familiar work and readable terms without confusing high technical skill with guaranteed income or an unchanging market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives me time to make choices in order rather than chase whatever is advertised as safe. I'd keep working in the familiar trade and ask the children what they actually wanted when decisions came. I'd still want any changed paid hours written down, not announced as a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when thinking AI arrived in 2036 and about 56 when the robots followed. I can't assume a pension or the children paying their own way would settle our mortgage. Two months saved gives us choices now, but the next contract still isn't confirmed and that keeps me anxious today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pursue the minimum-hours agreement now, assuming nothing until written terms protected the current weekly wage. I'd save 30 monthly from packed lunches only after food costs and essential bills, keeping the two-month reserve separate from any course advert. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs and apply for posted crew-lead work only if hours failed our budget, leaving only under the same signed pay, guaranteed-hours, travel and agreed care conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the near-term gap, with less rush about the machine dates. I'd like time to improve the arrangement without pretending I enjoy a new screen. A longer warning can help me decide without changing the bank balance tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the later care condition mean with older children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking the actual family needs then and agreeing any changed shifts with my partner. I wouldn't assume a school pickup still existed, or assume all family responsibilities had vanished. We'd use our real life, not keep today's timetable printed for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a course ever be part of your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If real paid work needed it, I'd ask about practical teaching and what it cost before deciding. I haven't chosen a course or an AI tool in this plan. I'd rather say that honestly than attach a training promise to a budget it hasn't met.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect capable robots around 2031 to remove a large part of ordinary installation income, while our current next contract is already uncertain. Written wages and paid hours, and job offers that actually cover the family after travel, would help. I'd also want any lender option explained with its eligibility and full cost before we changed anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a skilled worker can still prefer a familiar method without being called incapable. My test book is familiar because I know how to check the work, not because the work is simple. I want a dependable wage arrangement more than a flattering story about my qualifications.

headlineQuote: My test book is familiar because I know how to check the work, not because the work is simple.
portrait: Victor, **43**, is a highly skilled crew lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and typical pay.
His **partner** works at a laundry; their two children and mortgage share a budget with two months saved and unconfirmed work.
He has **never used AI**, preferring paper evidence and practical methods without denying either his own competence or later robot capability.
His **applications and agreements** require written affordable pay, guaranteed paid hours, travel costs and actual partner-agreed care rather than assumed job security.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before he expects robot-era installation losses, on top of the household's current unconfirmed-contract worry.
whatWouldHelp: Written **wages and paid hours** would support dependable household plans.
Affordable **job offers** and lender terms need travel, care agreement, eligibility and full costs checked before decisions.
